name: Authoritarian Capitalism
summary: Authoritarian capitalism pairs a market economy and private property with a strong, unaccountable government that restricts dissent and civil liberties. Its defenders argue that order, discipline and a capable leadership deliver growth and legitimacy more reliably than liberal democracy. The state steers investment through state-owned firms and strategic policy while using prosperity to secure public acquiescence.
scope: Represents the contemporary regime model of a market economy under an authoritarian state as its defenders and scholars describe it: Singapore under Lee Kuan Yew and the Asian-values argument, China after the 1978 reforms (Deng Xiaoping's reform line), and Putin's Russia as analysed by Aaron Friedberg. Pinochet's Chile, Dengist socialism and Putinism have their own profiles, and Gulf monarchies are treated as outlying cases. It is a regime type with ideological defenders rather than a codified doctrine, so many answers are inferred and the Chinese strand's official Marxism-Leninism is not taken as the model's own view.

keyFigures.name: Lee Kuan Yew
keyFigures.role: Singapore's long-time prime minister and leading advocate of order-first development and Asian values

keyFigures.name: Deng Xiaoping
keyFigures.role: Architect of China's market reforms under continued Communist Party rule

sources.title: Authoritarian capitalism
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: Definition, examples, defenders and critics, themes of markets, state firms, protectionism and regime stability.

sources.title: Uphold the Four Cardinal Principles (1979)
sources.author: Deng Xiaoping
sources.usedFor: A Marxist-Leninist speech by the architect of China's reforms: Party leadership, socialist rather than bourgeois democracy, condemnation of disruptive protest; also its affirmation of class struggle and proletarian dictatorship. It does not discuss markets.

sources.title: Lee Kuan Yew quotations
sources.author: Wikiquote (compilation of Lee's speeches and interviews)
sources.usedFor: Lee's statements on democracy and development, the press, family, meritocracy, one-party rule and self-reliance.

sources.title: Asian values
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: Primacy of group over individual, Bangkok Declaration, sovereignty and the cultural-relativist argument.

sources.title: State capitalism
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: State-owned enterprises, state direction of investment, retained wage labour and profit.

sources.title: Excerpts from talks given in Wuchang, Shenzhen, Zhuhai and Shanghai (1992)
sources.author: Deng Xiaoping
sources.usedFor: Deng's reform-era case that a market economy is not capitalism, growth of productive forces as the criterion, foreign-funded firms, praise of Singapore's strict order, and continued Marxist commitments.

sources.title: The Authoritarian Challenge: China, Russia and the Threat to the Liberal International Order
sources.author: Aaron L. Friedberg (Sasakawa Peace Foundation, 2017)
sources.usedFor: Scholarly account of 'nationalist authoritarian capitalism' in China and Russia: concentrated power without independent legislatures or judiciaries, state capitalism with market prices, global integration, nationalism and patriotic education, surveillance, NGO and internet control, rejection of universal values.

sources.title: Anti-Secession Law
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: China's 2005 law authorising non-peaceful means against Taiwanese secession.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Lee called Singapore a nanny state he was proud of, but its health model stresses mandatory individual savings and co-payment over a free state service, so support is tepid and inferred.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Singapore has no minimum wage and the model prizes labour competitiveness and self-reliance; the sources never address the question directly.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: The model keeps a market economy and private property, but with heavy state steering, so adherents back markets as the engine without calling them better than governments across the board.

public-ownership.rationale: State-owned enterprises and sovereign funds are prominent in China and Singapore, but the system also keeps private firms, so adherents split on public ownership of utilities.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Singapore's low-tax, pro-investment record suggests resistance to steeply higher taxes on the rich, though the sources give no explicit statement.

unions-good.rationale: Lee accepted Singapore's own cooperative unions while rejecting adversarial British-style unionism, and the model tolerates only state-aligned labour bodies, so adherents value unions only on those terms.

property-fundamental.rationale: Private property is a defining feature in the description of the system, though the state can override it for strategic or political ends, so it is not held as nearly inviolable.

regulate-corporations.rationale: The state directs and disciplines business to serve national goals, yet protects favoured firms; adherents are split on tighter regulation as such.

cut-welfare.rationale: Lee praised self-reliance and savings schemes over handouts but also defended a paternal state; adherents are divided on cutting welfare outright.

worker-ownership.rationale: The model rests on private and state ownership with wage labour; collective worker ownership plays no role in its programme.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Friedberg documents extensive surveillance in China and Russia justified as fighting crime and terrorism, and Lee defended state intrusion into private lives as necessary for progress.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Inferred from the model's disciplined social order and Lee's defence of state intrusion into private life; drug policy is not discussed in the sources.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: The model restricts speech to protect social harmony and stability, so legal limits on hate speech fit, though the motive is order rather than anti-hate principle.

strong-leader.rationale: Lee said the government decides what is right regardless of what people think, and Friedberg notes both China and Russia are led by popular 'maximum leaders' with concentrated power.

state-harmful.rationale: The system is defined by a strong authoritarian state guiding the economy, so it rejects the claim that the state is unnecessary.

limit-guns.rationale: Singapore and China tightly restrict firearms as part of an orderly society; the sources imply support, not a formal doctrine.

empower-police-military.rationale: Deng calls for strong organisation, discipline and stern dealing with disorder, which implies strengthening the security apparatus.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Asian-values advocates stress family and public morality, suggesting disapproval of legalised sex work, though Singapore tolerates regulated forms.

decide-locally.rationale: Deng demands strong centralised leadership and unified direction; the model is centralised rather than devolved.

rehabilitation.rationale: Lee defended detention without trial and corporal punishment, so adherents are inferred to lean towards punishment over rehabilitation.

traditional-family.rationale: Lee called the family the building brick of society that endures while governments come and go.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Asian-values rhetoric and the ruling parties' social conservatism mean same-sex marriage is not supported, though the economic focus makes it a lesser concern.

abortion-legal.rationale: Adherents are split: Singapore long allowed abortion for population and pragmatic reasons while China restricts by family policy, and Asian values give no clear line.

more-religion-public.rationale: Deng's Party is officially atheist and Singapore enforces secular management of religion, so a larger public religious role is not sought.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: The model favours merit and national stability over group-based remedies, though Singapore runs ethnic housing quotas for harmony; the evidence is indirect.

gender-social-construct.rationale: The sources do not address the question; adherents' emphasis on family and tradition points one way while state modernism points another.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Lee said the mass media should reinforce, not undermine, the country's cultural values.

gradual-change.rationale: Deng and Lee prize stability and order, accepting controlled step-by-step reform led from above rather than sudden disruption.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Singapore actively imports labour and talent while China is closed to immigration; adherents are split and the sources are silent.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: The 1993 Bangkok Declaration stressed sovereignty and non-interference, so adherents resist strengthening supranational bodies.

free-trade.rationale: Singapore is an open trader while China and Russia use protectionism and industrial policy; the model is not committed to free trade on principle.

nation-first.rationale: Proponents argue the model rests on nationalism and protectionism and puts national interest and regime stability first.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: The Bangkok Declaration emphasises sovereignty and non-interference, so intervention on human-rights grounds is disfavoured.

open-borders.rationale: Centralised state control, order and national interest rule out open borders as a goal.

limit-growth.rationale: Economic growth is the model's central justification, since improving living standards is said to secure regime legitimacy.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Not addressed in the sources; state capacity could implement drastic action, but growth priority works against it.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Modernisation through science and technology is central to Deng's Four Modernizations; the broader claim is inferred.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Modernisation and energy security priorities imply support, but the sources do not discuss nuclear power.

revolution-justified.rationale: Deng treats challenges to the Party's leadership as threats to stability to be dealt with sternly; the model is counter-revolutionary toward its own order.

experts-over-public.rationale: Lee advocated rule by able, well-paid officials selected on merit and said the government decides what is right irrespective of public opinion.

central-planning.rationale: The system is a market economy under state direction, not a centrally planned one; adherents think planning alone is inferior.

socialized-markets.rationale: Markets with private ownership and state firms are accepted, but the worker-owned requirement is not part of the model.

land-value-tax.rationale: Singapore owns most land and leases it, but no source ties the model to a land-value tax replacing others.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Singapore abolished estate duty in 2008 to attract wealth, and the model favours investment-friendly taxes; inferred.

basic-income.rationale: Lee stressed work, savings and self-reliance, so an unconditional income would be unwelcome; inferred.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Protectionism appears in descriptions of the model alongside nationalism, and states steer strategic industries behind barriers.

state-directs-investment.rationale: State capitalism names Lee's Singapore as a case of state control over credit and investment, and Friedberg describes states backing national champions and strategic sectors.

widespread-small-property.rationale: The model combines large state and private firms rather than aiming for wide small-owner distribution; inferred.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: State capitalism keeps wage labour and capital accumulation, and the model's market economy depends on money, so abolishing them is rejected.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: The state steers credit and the economy through state institutions, so abolishing the central bank is opposed.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Singapore's tripartite NTUC arrangement is corporatist, but China and Russia differ, so adherents split.

one-party-rule.rationale: Deng upheld the Party's leadership as essential; Lee said the PAP is the government. Yet the guiding ideology need not be a single correct creed in every variant.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Saudi Arabia is listed as an example, but most adherents run republics; the question is not central to the model.

democracy-best.rationale: Lee said democracy has rarely brought good government in developing countries; adherents deny that democracy is best when voters choose badly.

direct-votes.rationale: Lee held that the government decides what is right regardless of popular opinion, so direct votes on laws are rejected.

workers-councils.rationale: Deng tied democracy to centralism and Party leadership, and Friedberg describes power held by a small ruling elite, which leaves no place for council-based power.

right-to-secede.rationale: China's Anti-Secession Law exists to oppose and check secession, and the model's centralised states put territorial unity above regional self-rule; other cases are not documented.

natural-rulers.rationale: Lee argued for governing by an able elite chosen by merit and paid well; this is meritocratic rather than hereditary.

political-violence-never.rationale: Deng's dictatorship over the enemy and Lee's detention without trial treat state coercion as legitimate, though violence by opponents is condemned; adherents lean disagree.

war-builds-character.rationale: The model prizes stability for economic development, so celebrating war is not part of it; inferred.

separate-church-state.rationale: Both China and Singapore keep religion under state oversight, which fits strict separation in practice; inferred.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: The model's authority rests on state and Party rather than scripture; the Gulf variant differs, hence low confidence.

private-courts-defense.rationale: The model centres a strong state that monopolises security and justice, so privatised courts and defence are rejected; no source discusses the idea.

military-superiority.rationale: Nationalism and great-power ambition are associated with the model, though Singapore adopts a small-state stance; inferred.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Singapore built a multiracial policy and China an official multi-ethnic line, so adherents do not seek an ethnically pure nation.

class-struggle-history.rationale: The Chinese strand still professes Marxism-Leninism, which Deng calls its guide to action, but Friedberg describes China as having traded it for nationalism and Lee's Singapore and Russia reject class analysis, so the model as a whole leans against.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Meritocracy and unequal rewards drive Lee's model; equal outcomes are rejected.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Centralised state authority over land and territory is favoured; the sources do not address the topic.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Asian-values advocates criticised Western hypocrisy, but no source commits them to reparations.

civilizational-union.rationale: The model stresses national sovereignty and its own cultural path; unions of civilizations are not a goal.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Asian values subordinate individual interest to the group, yet profit-seeking is encouraged in the economy, so adherents are torn.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Lee described Asian values as the primacy of group interests over individual interests, and Friedberg notes that both regimes stress the primacy of the collective; duties are not named as such.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: The sources are silent; growth priority conflicts, while state-led greening is possible.

limit-population.rationale: China's one-child era supports limits while Singapore later pushed births; adherents split.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Scholars describe the model's legitimacy as resting on delivering economic growth, which presupposes industrial development; the claim itself is not discussed.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Modernisation is welcomed but controlled by the state for stability, so disrupting institutions is unwelcome.

human-enhancement.rationale: The sources do not address it; state control of biotech is likely, so adherents are split.

algorithmic-government.rationale: China uses algorithmic governance tools but the sources do not state it as a doctrine; split.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: The model subordinates liberties to security and surveillance, so encryption the state cannot break is opposed.

restore-past-order.rationale: Growth and modernisation are the priority, with tradition used selectively; progress outranks restoration.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Deng's pragmatic reform line judged policy by outcomes; Lee similarly valued what works, though Party principles remain fixed.

direct-action.rationale: Deng condemned sit-down and hunger strikes, obstructing traffic and raids on Party offices as disorder by trouble-makers, rejecting extra-institutional pressure on the state.

means-match-ends.rationale: Not a concern of the model; it accepts authoritarian means for development ends.

return-to-foraging.rationale: The model's legitimacy rests on industrial growth, so returning to foraging is rejected; no source discusses it.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Specialised firms and wage labour are part of state and private capitalism, so abolishing the division of labour is rejected; no source discusses it.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Pay and profit remain the basis of distribution, with merit rewarded by higher pay as Lee argued for officials, so distribution by need is rejected.

production-for-use.rationale: State capitalism retains production for profit alongside state firms, so replacing profit with use is not part of the model.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Profit-making firms, including foreign-funded ones Deng welcomed, are treated as legitimate, so the Marxist exploitation thesis is not part of the model.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Deng held in 1979 and 1992 that socialism needs the dictatorship of the proletariat, but Friedberg describes China's legitimacy as now nationalist rather than communist and Singapore and Russia reject class rule, so the model splits by strand and leans against.

collective-farming.rationale: China decollectivised farming in the reform era, and the model is market-based.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Defenders present capitalism as compatible with stable rule and global trade, so the claim that it inevitably breeds war is not theirs; no source discusses it directly.

taxation-theft.rationale: The model relies on a strong state that taxes and directs the economy, so this libertarian claim is rejected; no source discusses it directly.

harm-principle.rationale: Lee acknowledged interfering in citizens' private lives and defended it as necessary for economic progress, rejecting a limit of state action to harm prevention.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Asian values give primacy to the group and community over the individual.

conscription.rationale: Singapore runs national service and China keeps conscription law, so adherents accept state power to conscript.

exit-over-voice.rationale: The model offers little voice, but Lee did not ground legitimacy in freedom of exit; the claim is a libertarian one that adherents do not adopt.

state-as-business.rationale: Lee ran Singapore like a corporation with high official pay and efficiency, but citizens as customers who can leave is not his framing.

positive-liberty.rationale: Lee's paternal state provides housing and savings, yet the sources do not state this as a theory of freedom; split.

media-academia-power.rationale: Lee said media should reinforce state values, implying the media is powerful; the specific claim is not stated.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Lee made remarks on group traits, but the claim is not a core doctrine and adherents split.

organic-representation.rationale: Singapore's NTUC and grassroots bodies resemble corporatism, but it is not a stated doctrine; split.

total-state.rationale: Authoritarian capitalism keeps private markets and civil society outside direct state management, so a total state is not the aim.

national-rebirth.rationale: Chinese rejuvenation rhetoric exists but Singapore and others do not share it; adherents split.

territorial-expansion.rationale: China and Russia assert claims while Singapore does not, so adherents are split.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: The model rests on Party and bureaucratic institutions, though personalist networks exist; inferred.

bound-labor.rationale: The model relies on wage labour in markets, so bound labour runs against it; no source discusses it.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Deng and Lee treat official truth as set by the state, but not in the postmodern sense; inferred.

universal-morality.rationale: Asian-values advocates deny that Western rights apply universally, claiming that values differ by culture.

single-common-good.rationale: Lee held that the government decides what is right for society and puts the group interest first, which fits a single common good, though pragmatism rather than reason alone grounds it.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: The sources do not address this; adherents are split.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: The sources do not address this; adherents are split.

revive-national-language.rationale: The sources do not address this; adherents are split.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Wage labour under firms controlled by owners or the state is the model; democratic vote in firms is not.

school-vouchers.rationale: Singapore uses state-run schools with subsidies; the model has no stated voucher position.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Singapore is known for fiscal prudence and reserves, but China uses stimulus; adherents lean to prudence.

economic-freedom.rationale: The model rests on the claim that market freedom can thrive and last without political freedom, so adherents reject the statement.

rule-by-example.rationale: Lee stressed honest, exemplary officials but also law and punishment; adherents split.

national-self-determination.rationale: The Bangkok Declaration emphasised national sovereignty, so each state's right to govern itself is supported.

force-without-un.rationale: The sources are silent; Russia and China diverge from Singapore.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Deng's official atheism favours rationalism but Asian values value tradition; split.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Singapore restricts benefits largely to citizens; inferred.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Lee emphasised self-reliance and work-based savings schemes over handouts.

class-collaboration.rationale: Lee contrasted Singapore's cooperative unions with adversarial British unionism, and Deng stressed unity and stability, so labour and capital are expected to cooperate.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Preserving cultural values is a stated aim, so heritage should not be sacrificed.

dominated-front.rationale: The sources do not call for a common anti-Western front, though Asian-values advocates challenged Western standards; split.

workers-nation.rationale: Workers are expected to serve the national project under Party or state guidance; inferred.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Family-centred Asian values suggest traditional roles, but both states promote women's workforce participation; split.

ban-interest.rationale: State control of credit allocation, which the model uses to steer investment, presupposes interest-bearing lending; no source discusses banning interest.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Singapore enforces multiracial integration policy, opposing segregation by law.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Deng speaks of democracy for the people and dictatorship over enemies, but adherents deny the state is just a ruling-class tool.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Russia and Gulf cases rely on hydrocarbons and growth priority supports it; inferred.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: China pursues assimilation while Singapore uses multiracial integration; split.

elite-replacement.rationale: This conspiracy claim has no place in the model's documented positions.

proportional-representation.rationale: Singapore's winner-take-all system favours stable dominant government, so adherents oppose a shift; inferred.

national-mission.rationale: China has not exported its system by creed, but adherents do argue it is a viable model; split.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Not addressed; the model does not frame society this way.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Lee's model claims to produce clean, efficient government through high pay and tough anti-corruption, so adherents deny that elites are corrupt in general.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Lee promoted eugenic-style incentives for graduates, but state discouragement of births for defect is not a core position.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Lee defended detention without trial and the state's coercive powers, so legal accountability for past killings is opposed.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Friedberg describes states that plan, intervene for national champions and protect strategic sectors, and the model gives the state a directing economic role, so a minimal state is rejected.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Singapore promotes racial harmony and integration rather than discouraging mixing.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Equal moral worth is not denied, but the model puts group duty over equal rights, so agreement is weak.

socialism-one-country.rationale: Deng's priority was building modernisation within China, which is the opposite of this thesis.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: The sources do not address this; split.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: A centralised state tends to want uniform law, but Singapore keeps Muslim family law; low confidence.

restrict-conversion.rationale: The sources do not address conversion; states regulate religion for stability, so split.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Nothing in the model concerns cattle slaughter and it is a religious-cultural question; adherents lean against banning on pragmatic grounds.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Singapore teaches religious knowledge in schools while China forbids religious instruction; split.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Lee said the government decides what is right regardless of popular opinion; legitimacy rests on performance rather than consent.

trade-surplus.rationale: Mercantilist and protectionist aims are linked to the model, as is China's export surplus.

population-transfer.rationale: Not an endorsed doctrine, though regimes have pressured minorities; low confidence.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Deng accepted state coercion against enemies and Lee detention without trial, so this libertarian principle is rejected.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Competitive markets and meritocracy are valued, but social harmony is stressed over struggle; mild agreement.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Friedberg notes both regimes strictly control political opposition, and Deng said those who attack Party leadership must be dealt with according to law.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: No source addresses this definition of freedom; it is inferred from the model's acceptance of concentrated discretionary power, as when Lee said the government decides what is right.

separated-powers.rationale: Friedberg describes power concentrated in a small elite unchecked by autonomous legislatures or independent judiciaries, and Lee said the PAP is the government and the government is the PAP.

vanguard-party.rationale: Deng's Party-led vision is vanguardist, but the capitalist variants do not share the revolutionary theory; split.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Lee backed housing and savings for citizens but put growth and merit first; split.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Singapore's public housing is sold to citizens on long leases, giving broad ownership that adherents defend.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Lee said Singapore's unions are different and that British-style trade unionism would bankrupt the country, and he took a hard line on the 1980 pilots' strike; legal restriction of strikes follows.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: The sources do not address it; split.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Lee argued that officials must be paid enough to attract able people from the professions, which implies selection by ability; lottery is not discussed.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Singapore actively manages diversity for harmony, implying concern but not claiming diversity is a problem; split.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Lee said in 1986 that Singapore has to lock people up without trial, and earlier denied that detention without charge is totalitarian.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: A directing state controls strategic prices in China; inferred.

party-controls-media.rationale: Lee wanted media subordinated to the needs of the nation, and the model restricts the press, though ownership can be private.

party-commands-army.rationale: China's Party commands the army while Singapore does not; split.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Lee argued that low salaries will not attract able men who succeed in the professions or business, so pay at an average worker's level is rejected.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Deng demands strict organisation and discipline in the Party.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: The Bangkok Declaration reaffirmed sovereignty and non-interference, and Friedberg notes the push for 'Internet sovereignty', so pooling sovereignty in supranational bodies is resisted; pooling is not discussed as such.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Strong executive control of the military is consistent with the model; inferred.

church-by-bishops.rationale: The sources do not address this; split.

clerical-rule.rationale: Deng and Lee put secular Party or government authority above clerics.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Nationalist loyalty to the state is central to the model as Friedberg describes it, so wishing one's own government defeated is rejected.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Lee wanted media to reinforce cultural values, which implies censoring art that harms them.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Leader tenure is not capped by principle in the model, as in China's Party leadership and Singapore's long premiership.

recall-officials.rationale: Recall gives popular power over rulers, which the model resists; inferred.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Singapore relies on alliances and partners while China has few; split.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Property markets exist and rental housing is not targeted.

people-in-arms.rationale: The state keeps a monopoly on arms.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Urban modernisation is the model; inferred.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: China pursues reunification while Singapore has no such goal; split.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: The model relies on educated meritocratic officials and technocrats.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Lee claimed culture determines destiny and some cultures do better, so cultural equivalence is doubted.

death-penalty.rationale: Singapore and China keep capital punishment, which Human Rights Watch lists among Singapore's repressive practices; no defender's statement is cited, so this rests on the regimes' practice.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Singapore teaches sex education with a conservative slant; adherents split.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Public morality and cultural values are protected by restrictive law in Singapore and China.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Singapore uses descent-based citizenship rules; inferred.

minority-language-support.rationale: Singapore supports four official languages while China pushes Mandarin; split.

religious-exemptions.rationale: The state demands general compliance; inferred.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Asian values favour conformity and harmony over individual eccentricity.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: The sources do not address this; split.

constituent-assembly.rationale: The party and leader set constitutional terms, not an elected assembly.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Lee said that democracy has rarely brought good government to new developing countries and defended state intrusion as needed for economic progress; scholars say such regimes rest their legitimacy on delivering growth.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: The model stresses self-reliance and sovereignty; inferred.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: China and Russia have their own while Singapore does not; split.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Party selection of leaders is the norm in the model; Singapore's elected presidency is ceremonial.

central-bank-independence.rationale: State direction of credit implies central banks answer to the leadership.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: The sources do not address this; split.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: The state may override property for national goals, so property is justified insofar as it serves the common good.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: Scholars call Soviet economy state capitalist but adherents have no position; split.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Growth and pragmatism take priority over precaution; inferred.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Both states keep religion under civil authority.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: The head of state is typically the party leader in the model.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: China's 2005 Anti-Secession Law formalises the use of non-peaceful means if Taiwan moves to secede, and the model's centralised states treat national unity as non-negotiable.

region-keeps-system.rationale: China's one country, two systems formula, from the Deng era, matches this.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Secular Party and state do not claim divine rulers.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Singapore's progressive but low rates mean no position; split.

character-from-environment.rationale: Lee emphasised both culture and heredity; split.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: The leadership is not bound by courts or constitutional limits in practice, as Lee said the government decides what is right.

space-expansion.rationale: The sources do not address this; split.

mixed-constitution.rationale: The model concentrates power rather than mixing; inferred.

leader-cult.rationale: China and Russia have leader imagery while Singapore does not; split.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: Deng says class struggle exists objectively in socialist society but should not be exaggerated, and he rejects the Cultural Revolution idea of seizing power from party leaders restoring capitalism; non-Chinese variants have no such doctrine.

land-redistribution.rationale: Property rights and markets are protected, so land confiscation is rejected.

refugee-return.rationale: The sources do not address this; split.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Russia makes such claims and Singapore does not; split.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Secular states in the main cases do not punish apostasy; the Gulf variant differs.

women-must-cover.rationale: Secular main cases do not mandate covering.

common-currency.rationale: Sovereignty emphasis weighs against shared currency.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Centralised unity is favoured over minority autonomy.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: The sources do not address this; split.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Deng's Marxist frame affirms it while Lee emphasised culture; split.

ban-cartels.rationale: State-backed champions and cartels are common in the model.

no-bailouts.rationale: State capitalism supports strategic firms with public money.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: The model rejects both constraint by courts and majority rule; split.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: Merit selection is preferred over quotas.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: The model trades actively despite protection; autarky is not sought.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: Binding standards impinge on sovereignty and competitiveness; adherents resisted social clauses.

moral-incentives.rationale: Lee argued that low salaries will not attract able men, showing reliance on material rewards; the model does not propose replacing them.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: The model is counter-revolutionary towards its own order, and Deng condemned efforts to overthrow Party leadership; guerrilla revolution is not discussed.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Meritocracy is rhetorically central, although elite families persist; weak agreement.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Cultural-values and patriotic education fit the model.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Not addressed; adherents criticised colonial paternalism but defend their own; split.

patriotic-education.rationale: Friedberg describes China's Patriotic Education Campaign, launched in 1991, as the vehicle of the regime's new nationalist legitimacy.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Singapore uses ethnic quotas in housing but stresses merit; split.

public-money-creation.rationale: State steering of credit points to public control of money but the sources do not commit; split.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Friedberg describes communist regimes mutating into stable authoritarian capitalist ones, and the model presents capitalism as viable without liberal democracy, which implies confidence in its adaptability.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Russia seeks influence in former Soviet space; China and Singapore differ; split.

delink-world-market.rationale: Friedberg stresses that China and Russia are deeply integrated into the global economy, and Deng welcomed foreign-funded firms, so delinking is rejected.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: This Marxist-Leninist thesis is not part of the model's documented positions; inferred from its acceptance of profit and wage labour.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: The state manages racial harmony by law, so private discrimination is not free; inferred.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: These states have written constitutions with rights chapters, but Friedberg notes that they protect neither civil liberties nor basic rights in practice, and Lee held that the government decides what is right.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: The sources do not address this; split.

elective-rulers.rationale: Rulers are selected by party or tightly managed elections.

minority-veto.rationale: Deng links democracy with centralism and discipline, so letting a minority block decisions is rejected; vetoes are not discussed directly.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Deng treats challenges to Party leadership as disorder to be handled by law, so a right of resistance is rejected; the specific idea is not discussed.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Parliament in Singapore is dominated by the executive party; split.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: The sources do not address it; split.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Use of animals is accepted with moderate welfare standards; inferred.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Lee's paternal state accepts a duty of the elite to citizens; inferred.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Deng and Lee want the populace to focus on development and stay out of opposition politics, but not withdraw from society.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: Adherents see mass media as a tool to reinforce values, not as pacification, and would deny this critical claim.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: Lee's culture and media policy shows consent engineering alongside force, but the theory is not stated; split.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Adherents hold the world economy can lift poor countries through integration and growth.

party-own-road.rationale: Deng's reform line chose a Chinese road without direction from Moscow.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Lee stressed self-reliance, although the models also attract foreign investment; mild agreement.

return-lost-territory.rationale: China and Russia press claims while Singapore does not; split.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: Not addressed; merit-based leadership is preferred.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Not addressed; the model does not make it foundational.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: The sources do not address this; split.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: The sources do not address this; split.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: The sources do not address this; split.

male-disadvantage-attention.rationale: The sources do not address this; split.

domestic-violence-symmetry.rationale: The sources do not address this; split.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Lee said what Asians value may not be what Americans or Europeans value, and Friedberg describes both regimes building belief systems rooted in their own histories as better suited to their circumstances.

military-guardian-role.rationale: The army is the Party's in China but not in Singapore; split.

filial-duty.rationale: The Asian values article lists filial piety and loyalty to family among the values Lee and others promoted.

office-by-exam.rationale: Lee argued for able officials paid enough to attract talent from the professions, and the model favours technocratic selection over election; examinations are not discussed directly.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: State-backed control of strategic firms is characteristic, and nationalism and protectionism appear in descriptions.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Deng's democracy under centralism and Party leadership and Lee's view that the government decides what is right both reject bottom-up control of leaders.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: Singapore's mandatory CPF savings accounts are a model case of individual accounts, though state-run, not private companies.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Singapore state-owns land with leases and China has state land ownership; but adherents do not hold use-tenure as such; split.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Parliaments approve budgets formally but are dominated by the leadership; split.

single-official-language.rationale: China promotes Mandarin while Singapore keeps four languages; split.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: China bars private ownership of land and Singapore allows some; split.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: Merit selection is central; unequal outcomes are not discrimination.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Asian values stress thrift and anti-materialism, while growth depends on consumption; split.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Non-interference is emphasised, though Russia has backed proxies; low.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Non-interference is emphasised; Russia and China have acted otherwise.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: Deng's Party-state stressed strong centralised leadership but the doctrine is a Marxist-Leninist one, and the capitalist variants do not use it; adherents split.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Russia and China have annexed or claimed territory and reject this view, while Singapore has no stance; adherents lean disagree.

corporate-influence.rationale: Defenders say the state steers business, so corporate lobbying is less the complaint than market capture by a party; inferred, adherents split.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: Regimes defending the model treat foreign-funded NGOs and media as threats to order and sovereignty; inferred from the Four Cardinal Principles and Asian-values stance.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: Lee Kuan Yew-style governments openly used family incentives to raise birth rates; inferred from that record.

residents-only-property.rationale: No documented line; control of land by the state exists but local residency limits are not a defining plank.

job-guarantee.rationale: Market-based, growth-first model favours flexible labour markets over a state job guarantee; inferred.

democratic-peace.rationale: Defenders reject the view that spreading liberal democracy brings peace, arguing order and development come first; inferred from the Asian-values argument.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: The model stresses duty to the state and social discipline, so a general right to disregard law is rejected; inferred.

non-intervention.rationale: Asian-values defenders invoke non-interference in internal affairs against Western pressure on human rights; inferred.

industrial-unions.rationale: Unions are subordinated to the party or state in the model; no stated view on industry versus craft organisation, so slightly negative on independent unions.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Not part of the doctrine; the model rests on performance legitimacy, not minority scapegoating.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Family and social stability are valued as pillars of order, so removing legal marriage is unlikely to be favoured; inferred.

public-access-to-information.rationale: Restricting dissent and controlling information is characteristic, so a legal right of access to government information is disfavoured.

local-production.rationale: The model prizes export-led integration into global markets rather than localism; inferred.

informal-organisation.rationale: Permanent, disciplined party structures are central, and informal groups outside them are treated as a threat; inferred from the Four Cardinal Principles.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Sovereignty and non-interference are stressed against international pressure, so national law ranks above international courts; inferred.

religious-nation.rationale: China and Singapore are officially secular or multi-faith; religious definition of the nation is not part of the model.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: Defenders such as Lee and Deng stress national sovereignty and non-interference, so ritual tribute is inferred as unwelcome, though pragmatic alignment with a stronger partner is common.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: Advocates of strong central direction favour state-led planning of investment over regional fiscal autonomy; Deng's reforms did let regions keep revenue, so this is an inference at most.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: A market economy with private property implies private personal belongings, but the statement's common-ownership clause is not the model's position, so support is only partial and inferred.

defeat-communism.rationale: The model includes post-1978 China, where the ruling party is communist, alongside anti-communist cases such as Cold War regimes, so adherents are genuinely split.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: Singapore-style systems mix state funding with private and co-payment delivery, and the model favours market tools, but the sources do not set out a doctrine on providers.

religion-illusion.rationale: Deng's Four Cardinal Principles come from Marxism, but the Singapore branch values religion and family as social glue, so adherents lean against while differing across branches.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: The model rests on market capitalism as the engine of growth and modernisation, which its defenders credit for lifting living standards.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: Defenders favour markets and existing family structures; a demand to transform the economic system for gender equality runs against the model, inferred from its core economics.

socialized-care.rationale: Lee championed family responsibility and self-reliance over state provision, so replacing private family care with public services is inferred as disfavoured.

purge-loanwords.rationale: Singapore's model embraces English as a working language for trade and the sources show no purism; inferred from its pragmatic, outward-looking economics.

treaties-binding.rationale: A strong, unaccountable government keeping flexibility in the public interest is inferred as rejecting treaties it cannot change alone; the sources do not address the question.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Private property, markets and a strong central state are core to the model, which stands against common-property self-governing communities.

majority-settlement.rationale: Singapore's Lee kept ethnic balance through housing quotas, which runs against steering majority settlement into minority regions, but other cases such as China differ; inferred.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: The model is capitalist in economics, so a third course is not what it claims, although its defenders do present it as a distinct path from liberal democracy.

historical-land-claim.rationale: The model's nationalist strand asserts historical claims, as in the Anti-Secession Law over Taiwan; other cases such as Singapore make no such claim, so this is inferred.

holocaust-denial.rationale: Not discussed in the sources; inferred that regime defenders do not endorse denial.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Adherents split: Singapore kept its colonial-era law while mixing tolerance in practice, China and Russia differ; the sources do not settle it.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Defenders argue order and stability require limiting dissent; Deng's Four Cardinal Principles condemn disruptive protest and Lee defended press and political controls.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: These are secular regimes that control religion for order, not to defend orthodoxy; inferred.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Colonial exploitation is outside the model's ideas; inferred from its emphasis on sovereignty and self-reliance.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: Inferred: these regimes are secular and cast armed religious obligation as a threat to order.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: The regimes themselves reject force against rulers; inferred from their emphasis on stability and party or leader authority.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Concentrated power without independent legislatures and tight NGO control point against direct participation.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: Dengist Marxism asserts class struggle as central while the capitalist model defends hierarchy; neither accepts intersectional analysis, inferred.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: Inferred from Asian-values emphasis on the family and group; the sources do not address gender identity.

assisted-dying.rationale: Inferred from the Asian-values stress on duty and social order; not directly addressed.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: Deng's pragmatism holds that a market economy is not capitalism and that growth is the criterion; it treats ideological labels as secondary.

alienated-labor.rationale: Dengist ideology is Marxist but affirms wage labour, profit and state-led growth; defenders do not accept an alienation critique of their model.

islam-incompatible.rationale: Defenders stress cultural relativism and sovereignty over universal values; Islam as a topic is not discussed, so it is a weak inference.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Authority is grounded in performance, order and in China the Party, not in God; Deng upholds Party leadership.

religious-dress-in-state.rationale: Secular states with patriotic education and state control of religion would restrict religious dress in institutions; inferred.

ban-nda-harassment.rationale: Concentrated, business-friendly regimes with weak courts rarely back limits on employers; inferred.

social-market-economy.rationale: State capitalism keeps strong state direction of firms and investment, which fits neither the social-market model nor laissez-faire; inferred.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: These states keep large armed forces and put sovereignty and security first, as the Anti-Secession Law shows.

rich-first.rationale: Deng's reform line justified uneven growth while productive forces developed and foreign-funded firms came in.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Great-power regimes such as China and Russia pursue independence from rival blocs; inferred, and Singapore is aligned.

missingStatements.text: Government officials should be paid market-level salaries so that able people are attracted and corruption is discouraged.
missingStatements.rationale: Lee argued that low salaries draw in hypocrites and fail to attract able men.
missingStatements.declined: Narrow administrative policy detail, not a defining position.

missingStatements.text: A government's legitimacy should rest mainly on its record of delivering prosperity and order rather than on elections.
missingStatements.rationale: Proponents argue rising living standards secure regime stability, and Lee said democracy has seldom brought good government to developing countries.

notes: Authoritarian capitalism is mainly a descriptive regime label, so adherents are defined by its defenders (Lee, Deng-era reformers) and by scholarly accounts of the shared model (Friedberg). The Chinese strand still professes Marxism-Leninism (Deng 1979 and 1992 uphold class struggle and the dictatorship of the proletariat), while Singapore and Russia do not, so Marxist statements are answered low-confidence as strand splits. Russian and Gulf variants would answer differently on nationalism, religion and territory. Wikiquote was used as a compilation of Lee's statements, not as an independent scholarly source.
